item.title: ISEFlow: a flow-based neural network emulator for improved sea level projections and uncertainty quantification
item.dc:creator: Peter Van Katwyk, Baylor Fox-Kemper, Sophie Nowicki, Hélène Seroussi, Karianne J. Bergen
item.description:
The Cryosphere — matched: ice sheet, Antarctica, Greenland, sea level, uncertainty quantification, emulator, machine learning, neural network
We developed ISEFlow, a new climate emulator model that predicts how melting ice sheets in Greenland and Antarctica will contribute to future sea levels. It uses advanced machine learning to capture complex ice processes, distinguish between different emission scenarios, and provide clearer estimates of uncertainty. This makes sea level projections more accurate and reliable, helping scientists and policymakers better plan for climate risks.

item.title: Timing of Ocean–Atmosphere Variability and Its Impacts on Central Patagonian Ice Sheet Since MIS 3: Insights From Multiproxy Marine Records
item.dc:creator: Lena Andrzejewski, Giuseppe Siani, Karim Lebeaupin, Sébastien Bertrand, Samuel Toucanne, P. Richard, … (+3)
item.description:
Paleoceanography and Paleoclimatology — matched: ice sheet, glacier, sea surface temperature, last glacial maximum, marine isotope stage, MIS stage
Glaciers in southern mid‐latitudes during the late Marine Isotope Stage 3 (MIS 3) were likely strongly influenced by ocean‐atmosphere connections. However, the orbital‐ and millennial‐scale variability of the Patagonian Ice Sheet (PIS) remains poorly constrained, largely due to the scarcity of terrestrial records from the western Andean margin and the limited availability of continuous, well‐dated marine archives. Here, we present two continuous multiproxy marine records from the central Patagonian margin spanning the end of MIS 3 to the present. Site MD07‐3119 (46°S) is influenced by proximal ice‐sheet melting, whereas site MD07‐3082 (49°S) reflects the broader regional evolution of the PIS. Based on a new chronological approach, our data from the two cores constrain the last maximum extent of the central western PIS to ∼26.5(+0.83)–25.5(−0.52) ka, prior to the Last Glacial Maximum defined between 24.9–19.7 ka. Furthermore, high‐resolution ln(Ti/K) data and sediment accumulation rates reveal five millennial‐scale events of enhanced terrestrial sediment input, with increase factors of 1.6–30, coinciding with freshwater inputs and cooling of sea surface water and interpreted as central PIS advances and retreats. These millennial‐scale glacier fluctuations are synchronous with those reported for the New Zealand ice field, which may be explained by associated sea surface temperature changes and shifts of the Southern Westerly Winds, likely driven by climate variability in the South Pacific via ocean‐atmosphere interactions.

item.title: Unlocking the unparalleled paleoclimate record of Antarctic blue ice areas
item.dc:creator: Veronica Tollenaar, Étienne Legrain
item.category: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
item.description:
Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences — matched: ice flow, Antarctic, Antarctica, paleoclimate, ice core, climate change
Ice uniquely provides direct samples of ancient atmosphere, enabling measurements of greenhouse gases contemporaneous to temperature reconstructions. Blue ice areas (covering 1% of the surface of Antarctica) hold a largely underexplored paleoclimate record that can extend beyond deep ice cores (that is, older than 1.5 My), covering periods in which global surface temperatures were similar to projected future temperatures. Blue ice areas expose ancient ice directly at the surface or at shallow depths due to net ablation and redirected ice flow, providing access to old ice at logistically reduced costs. However, the analysis and interpretation of blue ice samples is challenging, given the complex flow patterns in these regions that result in tilted layers, inversions and discontinuities in the stratigraphy, and complex ice–bedrock interactions. This paper presents a succinct review of state-of-the-art blue ice research, placed in the context of established ice core research, and argues that to advance the search for ancient ice, efforts in blue ice areas should focus on: i) collecting dated surface samples, ii) investigating the relationship between the age of the ice and other datable evidence, such as moraines, dust layers, meteorites, and exposed bedrock, and iii) developing models that can capture the typically disturbed or discontinuous stratigraphy. Together with advances in analytical techniques that address, for example, contamination and absolute dating, these efforts could lead to the recovery of the oldest ice on Earth, unravel warm climates of the past, and improve future climate change projections.

item.title: Climate-related signals in the GV7-C ice core from East Antarctica for 1782–2013 CE: potential relevance to climate and teleconnections between the tropics and Antarctica
item.dc:creator: Yalalt Nyamgerel, Yeongcheol Han, Soon Do Hur, Hyemi Kim, Songyi Kim, Jangil Moon, … (+2)
item.description:
Earth System Dynamics — matched: Antarctic, Antarctica, polar, ice core
This research explores climate patterns recorded in Antarctic ice over the past two centuries. By analyzing ice layers, we identified connections between Antarctica's climate and tropical ocean conditions. Results show changing influences over time and highlight the Indian Ocean's key role in Antarctic snowfall. This improves understanding of how polar and tropical climates interact, crucial for future climate predictions.

item.title: Basin-Scale Nonlinear Dynamics of Thermohaline Ocean Circulation. Part I: Theory
item.dc:creator: Conner W. Lester, Dylan E. McNamara, Till J. W. Wagner
item.description:
arXiv physics.ao-ph — matched: tipping point, bifurcation, ocean circulation
arXiv:2611.33383v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Earth's thermohaline ocean circulation may support multiple equilibria and abrupt transitions. Similar bifurcation structures for different ocean models suggest common underlying dynamics across the model hierarchy. Here we propose a unifying framework from tracer conservation, in which surface fluxes are balanced by dissipative and advective tracer transport. We express this flux balance through a large-scale tracer gradient and a transport efficiency that measures how strongly circulation displaces the tracer field from its no-flow "conductive" state. The flux balance quantifies the transport contributions that sustain each circulation state and give rise to abrupt transitions. In a three-dimensional ocean-basin model, we find nonlinear salinity advection dominates the collapse threshold and linear dissipation dominates the recovery threshold. Temperature has additional dissipation from surface restoring, making thermal fluxes more dissipation-dominated than salinity fluxes. The tracer contrasts and boundary layers that a given circulation generates produce distinct transport regimes, approximately quadratic in circulation strength for weak flow and linear for strong flow. With a simple circulation closure, the flux balance reduces to longstanding box-model bifurcation results for the weak and strong flow regimes. Thus, by expressing thermohaline bifurcations through basin-scale transport, this framework connects box-model insight to the continuous equations. Furthermore, as this framework exposes the transport processes that balance a changing forcing, it provides constraints on a thermohaline ocean state and its trend toward tipping that overturning strength alone does not. In Part II, we develop flux-balance closures to forecast such tipping points.

item.title: A comprehensive global ocean radiocarbon dataset (1700–2024) for climate applications
item.dc:creator: Nabir Mamnun, Branwen Williams, Rena Mukherjee, Roberta L. Hansman, Rolf Sonnerup, Nikita Tournebise, … (+2)
item.description:
Earth System Science Data — matched: ocean circulation, radiocarbon, carbon cycle
Radiocarbon measurements in the ocean are key to studying ocean circulation, gas exchange and the carbon cycle, but they are sparse and scattered across many sources. We combined about 68,500 measurements from ship-based seawater samples (1955–2024) and biogenic carbonates (corals and shells, 1700–2020) into one quality-checked, openly available dataset. The dataset provides the most comprehensive record of ocean radiocarbon over the industrial period, including impacts of nuclear bomb tests.

item.title: OMNIE-Nutrients: A Global Gridded Ocean Nutrient Dataset (1965–2022) Derived from a Neural Network Emulator and In-Situ Observations
item.dc:creator: Said Ouala, Zouhair Lachkar
item.description:
Earth System Science Data — matched: emulator, machine learning, neural network
Preprint under review for ESSD (discussion: open, 0 comments) OMNIE-Nutrients is a global gridded dataset of marine macronutrients (nitrate, phosphate, silicate) spanning 1965–2022. It integrates sparse in situ observations with machine-learning-emulated profiles derived from hydrographic data, expanding the effective observational network by an order of magnitude. These interpolated fields eliminate severe artifacts and historical sampling biases prevalent in standard climatologies, providing a robust baseline for evaluating biogeochemical variability.

item.title: Lipid biomarker signatures of charophytes and submerged vascular macrophytes
item.dc:creator: R.N. Santos, Bernhard Aichner, D.B. Nelson, S. Hilt, S.N. Ladd
item.description:
Organic Geochemistry — matched: paleoclimate, proxy
Aquatic lipid biomarkers are widely used in paleoclimate and paleolimnological reconstructions, yet modern calibrations often treat aquatic plants as a single source group. This assumption may be problematic in lakes where charophytes and submerged vascular macrophytes co-occur, as these groups are physiologically distinct. Here, we evaluated whether these two groups can be distinguished using lipid distributions, compound-specific stable isotopes, and bulk geochemistry. We analyzed 82 samples from 20 lakes in northeast Germany, comprising 44 charophytes and 38 submerged vascular plants. Submerged vascular plants had substantially higher lipid concentrations than charophytes, particularly for mid-chain n- C 23 and n- C 25 alkanes. Abundance-weighted mixing tests indicate that even a small presence of vascular-macrophytes could cause them to dominate the aquatic n -alkane pool. The routinely used sedimentary ‘P aq ’ index is sensitive to submerged vascular plant input but should not be interpreted as a quantitative measure of total submerged aquatic biomass or productivity. Fatty acid abundances were less different among plant groups, indicating that fatty acids may contain a stronger charophyte contribution than n -alkanes. Charophyte n -alkanes and fatty acids were systematically less 2 H-depleted than those of submerged vascular macrophytes, whereas phytol δ 2 H values were indistinguishable between groups, making the n -C 16 fatty acid/phytol δ 2 H offset significantly larger in charophytes. This suggests that lipid δ 2 H values are strongly influenced by taxonomic differences in biosynthetic fractionation and metabolic processes, rather than source-water δ 2 H values alone. Bulk organic matter data provided useful support but were not diagnostic on their own. Aquatic biomarkers should therefore be interpreted within a multi-proxy framework.

item.title: Future Changes in ENSO Modulation of the Ocean Coupling Potential Intensity of Tropical Cyclones over the Western North Pacific
item.dc:creator: Qimeng Wu, Hailong Liu, Lei Zhou
item.description:
Journal of Climate — matched: CMIP, radiative forcing, ensemble
Anthropogenic warming may alter the El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO) modulation of the tropical cyclone thermodynamic intensity limit over the western North Pacific (WNP). Using a 26-model CMIP6 ensemble, we examine projected changes in ENSO-related Ocean Coupling Potential Intensity (OC_PI) during June–November for 2066–2100 relative to 1980–2014. The ensemble projects stronger thermodynamic suppression during El Niño and enhanced favorability during La Niña, with the magnitude increasing under stronger radiative forcing. Linear factor decomposition indicates that these changes are associated primarily with the CAPE-based air–sea thermodynamic-disequilibrium contribution, whereas the thermodynamic-efficiency contribution, associated with the temperature contrast between the oceanic heat source and atmospheric outflow, remains comparatively small. Changes in ENSO amplitude alone do not fully explain the projected upper-ocean response. After accounting for amplitude scaling, the upper-100-m mean temperature (T100) response remains increasingly negative during El Niño and positive during La Niña under the stronger forcing scenarios. Intermodel relationships provide phase- and forcing-dependent support for an association between enhanced background thermal stratification and the adjusted upper-ocean response, with clearer evidence during La Niña. A stronger upper-ocean vertical temperature gradient can amplify T100 anomalies associated with comparable ENSO-related isotherm displacements. The upper-ocean temperature changes are also closely related to changes in ocean-controlled saturation CAPE, while the boundary-layer response is weaker. Sensitivity tests using alternative ENSO thresholds and upper-ocean averaging depths preserve the principal phase-dependent response. These results highlight the importance of subsurface ocean structure for projections of ENSO-related changes in the WNP tropical cyclone thermodynamic environment.

item.title: Convolution based techniques for computing self attraction and loading in MOM6
item.dc:creator: Anthony Chen, He Wang, Brian K. Arbic, Robert Krasny
item.description:
Geoscientific Model Development
Self Attraction and Loading (SAL) is an important force that affects many oceanic motions, including tides. Computing SAL is challenging and ocean models neglected to include the impacts of SAL for a long time. Recent work has proposed a method for incorporating the effects of SAL, but the method has several limitations that limit the accuracy. This work proposes an alternative method. Tests of this new method in an ocean model indicate that it reduces the amount of error in the modeled tides.

item.title: LCS.jl v1.0: a high-performance, multi-platform computational model in Julia for turbulent particle-laden flows
item.dc:creator: Taketo Tominaga, Ryo Onishi
item.description:
Geoscientific Model Development
Turbulent multiphase flow simulations of cloud droplet growth are computationally demanding. We developed LCS.jl (Lagrangian Cloud Simulator in Julia), which runs efficiently on CPUs and GPUs from one codebase. A prefix-scan algorithm reduced particle communication cost by about 88 %. The model achieved about 70 % strong-scaling efficiency on 256 GPUs and about 80 % weak-scaling efficiency on 216 GPUs. These results show that LCS.jl provides a portable and scalable platform for such simulations.

item.title: Interactive land in E3SM process-level models: impacts of land–atmosphere coupling in SCM and DP-SCREAM
item.dc:creator: Peter A. Bogenschutz, Yunyan Zhang, Hsi-Yen Ma, Cheng Tao, Shaocheng Xie
item.description:
Geoscientific Model Development
Weather and climate models are often tested using simplified simulations that prescribe exchanges between the land and atmosphere. We developed a method that allows these interactions to evolve naturally and evaluated it using observations from field sites in the United States and Brazil. We found that realistic land-atmosphere interactions are important for reproducing temperature and cloud biases, while many rainfall errors originate within the atmosphere model itself.

item.title: Compression Safeguards: building trust into lossy data compression
item.dc:creator: Juniper Tyree, Robert Underwood, Clément Bouvier, Daniel Köhler, Tim Reichelt, Peter Dueben, … (+3)
item.description:
Geoscientific Model Development
Many scientists use computers to simulate our world. This is producing too much data. Data can be made smaller using lossy compression. But many scientists fear losing important details and avoid it. We created Compression Safeguards to protect scientists and make lossy compression safe. First, scientists say what’s important in their data. Then the Safeguards correct the compressed data so that nothing important is lost. We test many examples: Safeguards protect but make the data less smaller.
